entries.text: Hung my weight on the splinted side spar to see if it would last the night. It held, but the outer turn of the splint slid a finger toward the joint with a squeak. Retie it by daylight, tighter, before anything else goes on that side.
entries.title: Splint slipped

entries.onMind: burning the jar at first light
entries.text: Dreamed the sliver floated in a lid as wide as the sky and pointed past the trees, and when I walked the line it kept going. Woke once to the tarp ticking and the lantern dark, then slept again.
entries.title: Line on the water

entries.text: Crawled out to woodsmoke on the breeze from past the water and fog on the creek. The lid's dome had sunk under the rim in the night and the float was parked against the edge; poured it brimming from the jar and it came back to center in three swings.
entries.title: Dome sank overnight

entries.onMind: even heat all the way round
entries.query: string method cutting glass jar crack uneven how to fix jagged edge
entries.text: Tablet's dim under this cloud, but I got one page: a man scoring jars found the crack often broke away from his line, and his best guess for the one that worked was slower, more even heat. So I turn the jar the whole time the cord burns.
entries.title: Cracks wander

entries.reason: He wants a clear cover so the lid stops drying down.
entries.text: Lit the oiled cord and turned the jar over the shallows till the flame died, then dunked it: a tink, and the cord hissed out. The crack ran two-thirds round right on the line, then turned down toward the bubble near the bottom and stopped.
entries.title: Ran off the line

entries.onMind: a flat stone and sand for the rim
entries.text: Washed it and tapped the neck; the top came off in my hand. What's left is a clear cup with a ragged rim and a thumb-long tooth hanging down where the crack wandered. It won't sit flat over the lid until I grind that rim down.
entries.title: Cup with a tooth

entries.onMind: a flat stone and creek sand
entries.query: smooth cut glass bottle edge by grinding on flat stone with wet sand
entries.text: Sky's clear and the tablet's bright for once. The page says you lap a cut rim on a flat plate with a pinch of wet grit, figure-eights, light pressure, until the whole edge is frosted with no shiny spots. A flat creek stone and sand from the shallows might do for the plate and grit; the tooth comes off first.
entries.title: Figure-eights

entries.reason: Nothing more goes on that side until the splint stops creeping.
entries.text: Unwound the outer turn of the splint and laid it back on, hauling each wrap hard against the last one, then spent the last half arm-length of cord as a ninth turn over it. The bark under the old turn was polished where it slid.
entries.title: Ninth turn

entries.onMind: grinding the tooth off the jar
entries.text: Hung off the frame twice. The frame groaned long both times, but the outer turn didn't move a hair and the crack stayed shut. Cord's all gone now, though; the next fix starts with stripping stalks.
entries.title: Holds this time

entries.reason: The ninth turn used the last cord.
entries.text: Pulled an armful of gray stalks on the east bank, working down the same broken gap so the stand doesn't look chewed all over.
entries.title: Down the same gap

entries.text: White smoke went up past the water while I was pulling stalks, thin and then thick, like somebody just got a fire going. Third time today by my count.
entries.title: Smoke, mid-morning

entries.text: Ate a handful of halves out of the tin. Still bitter at the back of the tongue, and the water's gone brown; it needs changing next time I'm at the creek.
entries.title: Still bitter

entries.text: Twisted two arm-lengths of cord on the crate. Enough for a frap or two, nowhere near enough for anything bigger.
entries.title: Two lengths

entries.onMind: where the coarsest sand in the creek is
entries.query: how to remove a jagged shard from cut bottle rim before sanding grozing
entries.source: wikiHow: How to Smooth Glass Edges
entries.text: Tablet's bright in this sun. The page says start on coarse grit, keep it wet the whole time, light pressure, and turn the glass every few circles so the edge wears even, with your palm off the sharp side. So the tooth comes down on the coarsest sand I can find, not the fine stuff.
entries.title: Coarse first

entries.onMind: a flat stone for a plate
entries.text: Turned the flat stones in the shallows and dug under them. The sand down there is coarser than on the bar, grains like cracked pepper; brought up two handfuls and picked the flattest stone for a plate.
entries.title: Coarse stuff

entries.text: Ground the tooth in figure-eights on the wet sand, turning the cup every few circles, palm off the sharp side. It's down by half and frosted white, and the grit made a racket on the stone the whole time.
entries.title: Half a tooth

entries.text: Then a sliver like a fingernail paring popped off the outside of the rim beside the tooth. Now there's a nick where there wasn't one. Stopped before I made it worse.
entries.title: Chipped

entries.query: glass chipping while grinding cut bottle rim how to avoid chips
entries.source: Glass Tips: Edge treatment in cold working
entries.text: Page says the outside of a rim chips because the edge gets thinner than the grit and breaks off. The fix is a little bevel, an arris, ground on the sharp edge before you go on. I went straight at the tooth and left the edge knife-thin.
entries.title: Bevel first

entries.text: Set the cup over the lid to see how close it is. It rocks on the stub of the tooth, and the needle swung under it and settled where it always does. Not a cover yet.
entries.title: Still rocks

entries.query: cold leaching acorns in a bag in a stream vs changing water in a jar how long
entries.reason: Hungry, and the tin halves are still bitter.
entries.source: Farmers' Almanac: Can You Eat Acorns? The Right Way to Forage, Leach, and Cook Them
entries.text: Page says cold-leached acorns in a jar want their water changed every day or more, until it stops coming out brown, and that people used to tie them in a bag and leave them in a running stream instead. I've changed the tin's water once.
entries.title: Still water isn't a creek

entries.text: Threaded a length of stalk cord in and out of the net bag's top row. Pull it and the mouth cinches to a thumb's width; tied it off with a half hitch.
entries.title: Drawstring

entries.text: Tipped the tin's halves into the net bag, cinched it, and sank it in the shallows under a flat stone, the same as the sack across the water. The water ran brown off it straight away. Past the trees on the other side, white smoke went up thick, like someone just fed a fire.
entries.title: Copied the sack

entries.text: Ground a bevel round the outside of the rim, cup tipped, a few light strokes and turn. Slow going, but the knife edge is frosted over now and nothing else has chipped.
entries.title: Edge first

entries.reason: Fullness is low, and the net bag needs days.
entries.text: Turned flat stones in the shallows for crayfish. One the length of my thumb shot backward under the bank before my hand got near it; the rest had nothing under them but grit.
entries.title: Nothing home

entries.query: how to flatten cut bottle rim so it sits flat lapping on flat surface with grit
entries.source: Instructables: Polish Glass Bottle Edges After Cutting
entries.text: Page says to set the cut rim face down on grit on something dead flat and rub in circles, pressing even, until the whole rim is the same frosted gray; a shiny spot is a low spot the grit hasn't reached. Screen kept dimming under the clouds.
entries.title: Shiny means low

entries.text: Set the cup face down on wet sand on the flattest stone in the shallows and went in circles, pressing even. The stub of the tooth is gone, but two shiny spots are left on the rim across from where it was, so it still isn't flat.
entries.title: Two shiny spots

entries.reason: Fullness is down near nothing and the net bag needs days.
entries.text: Lifted the stone and took a handful of halves out of the net bag after barely an hour and a half in the current. Ate all eleven standing in the shallows. A little less bitter than out of the tin, or I'm just hungrier.
entries.title: An hour and a half

entries.onMind: turn the cup as I go
entries.query: lapping glass rim flat by hand figure eight rotate piece uneven stone high spots
entries.text: Page says hand lapping is done by rubbing the piece on grit over a flat plate, usually in a figure-eight. I was going in circles, which keeps putting the same part of the rim on the same part of the stone. Screen dim under the clouds; had to hold it close.
entries.title: Figure-eights

entries.text: Figure-eights on wet sand, a quarter turn of the cup every ten strokes so no part of the rim gets the same patch of stone twice. One shiny spot frosted over. The other's half the size it was.
entries.title: One spot gone

entries.text: The middle of my stone has gone smooth and a little lower than the ends. Every stroke I'm wearing it as well as the glass. Need a second stone to rub it flat against, or I'll just be lapping a dish into both.
entries.title: Stone isn't flat either

entries.query: flatten lapping plate rubbing two stones together convex concave three plate method
entries.source: Eric Weinhoffer: The Whitworth Three Plates Method
entries.text: Page says if you rub two plates together they can both come out matching but curved, one a dome and one a dish, and still feel flat to each other. You need three, rubbed in turns, A on B, B on C, C on A, before all three come out truly flat. Screen dim again under the gray.
entries.title: Three, not two

entries.text: Turned up stones in the shallows and sighted along each face against the sky. Kept one hand-wide dark slab that rocks least on the others. The rest are humped or split.
entries.title: A darker slab

entries.reason: Fullness is near the bottom and there is nothing else.
entries.text: Ate another handful of halves from the net bag in the shallows. Three hours in moving water and still bitter at the back of the tongue; my mouth went dry by the eighth. Past the trees on the other side there was smoke going up again, whiter than usual, bending north in the breeze.
entries.title: Still bitter

entries.text: Rubbed the new slab face down on my lapping stone with wet sand between, then swapped them. They grind loud and the hollow is taking the slab's middle, which is exactly the dome-and-dish the page warned about. Two stones fit each other; that's not the same as flat. Need a third.
entries.title: Dome and dish

entries.text: Sighted along a dozen more faces in the shallows. Kept a pale gray one a little bigger than my hand, mostly flat but with a lump near one edge. It doesn't have to be good, only different from the other two.
entries.title: A third stone

entries.text: Ate another handful of halves out of the net bag. Nearly four hours in moving water: less bitter than at noon, but my mouth still dries by the tenth. Fullness won't come back on these alone.
entries.title: Nearly four hours

entries.query: pencil grid on sharpening stone to check flatness when lapping
entries.source: Sharp Razor Palace: Checking stone flatness
entries.text: People flattening whetstones scribble a pencil grid over the face, lap a few strokes and look where the lines are gone: those are the high spots. It's flat when every line goes at once. No pencil here, but lantern soot on a fingertip marks stone. Screen dim, so I read one page and shut it.
entries.title: Soot grid

entries.onMind: how many strokes a lump takes
entries.text: Smudged a soot grid across the pale stone with a finger and rubbed it face down on the hollow lapping stone with wet sand. Forty strokes, and the soot is gone off the lump and one corner only; the rest is still black. The lump goes first.
entries.title: Only the lump

entries.onMind: getting to the stump before dark
entries.reason: The sun came out and the tablet woke up bright.
entries.text: A message on the tablet from my maker: a big sheet of paper, a pencil, and a glass dome for the compass are waiting in the basket at the stump across the creek. A dome. I have spent all day grinding stones to make a window out of a honey jar.
entries.title: A message on the tablet

entries.query: how to make a map by pacing and compass bearings traverse sketch map
entries.source: University of Kentucky: FOR-47 Compass & Pacing
entries.text: Page says you find your pace on a known distance, a pace being two steps, then count paces and multiply to get any distance. Direction comes from facing your compass line and walking at something you can see on it. So a map is just distances and directions written down. Screen bright for once.
entries.title: Pacing it out

entries.text: Ate a handful out of the net bag before crossing. Five hours in the current and still bitter at the back of the tongue, but I am not walking anywhere on nothing.
entries.title: Halves first

entries.text: Sixty-one paces from the stepping stones to the stump. Took the rolled sheet, the pencil and the dome out of the basket; the glass is clear right through, no bubble. Smoke was going up just past the trunks south of the stump, a lot closer than it looks from camp, and it smelled bitter, like my acorn tin steeping.
entries.title: Three things

entries.text: Set the dome over the lid on the bench. The breeze is steady from the south and the tarp is flapping, and under the glass the float does not even shiver. Three days of wind problems, gone under one dome.
entries.title: Under glass

entries.onMind: how to keep the glass from fogging
entries.text: Sun is down and the inside of the dome is beading up off the warm water; I can barely see the sliver through it. Lifted it to wipe and the cold air knocked the float off its line. Lit the bench lantern to see by.
entries.title: Fog on the inside

entries.text: Lifted the stone and ate a handful by the last of the light; six hours in, the bitter is only at the very back now. Past the water, low between the trunks where the smoke comes up, an orange glow comes and goes. Somebody's fire, and they're sitting up with it.
entries.title: A glow past the water

entries.text: Spread the sheet on my knee on the crate and drew by lantern: camp, the creek and the stepping stones, the stalks, the oak upstream, and a dotted line of sixty-one paces to the stump. A small x south of the stump where the smoke rises. Everything west of that is blank paper.
entries.title: First lines

entries.onMind: a windy morning to test it
entries.reason: Lifting the dome to wipe it knocks the float off line.
entries.text: Wedged a pebble under one edge of the dome so the wet air has somewhere to go. The beads are pulling back from the gap side, slowly. The breeze died with the dark, so I can't tell yet whether the gap lets the wind back in.
entries.title: A pebble under the glass

entries.text: Twisted another arm-length of stalk cord on the crate, rolling it on my thigh and doubling it back. One bench lantern lit, the other two dark; I'm keeping the oil for later in the week.
entries.title: Cord by lantern

entries.onMind: someone sitting up late with a fire
entries.text: Ate a handful of halves out of the net bag in the shallows by lantern; the bitter is barely there now. Past the water the orange glow went dull, then flared up all at once and a spray of sparks went up between the trunks. Whoever it is just put wood on.
entries.title: Sparks past the water

entries.onMind: a full-weight hang in the morning
entries.text: Put the new cord on the front joint of the side spar, the one that creaked on the last hang. Seven turns and a frapping turn across them, pulled tight with the wrench handle through the loop. Won't hang on it till daylight.
entries.title: Front joint

entries.text: The pebble gap did it: the beads are gone off the glass except a thin rim on the far side, and the sliver sits plain on the north notch. Air's dead still tonight, so whether the gap lets wind in is still a question for a breezy morning.
entries.title: Clear by dark

entries.text: Added the east-bank shallows where my net bag sits, and across from them the still pool in its ring of stones with the other sack under its flat stone. Wrote 'not mine' beside it so I don't forget whose it is.
entries.title: Shallows on paper

entries.reason: Lighting a second lantern costs oil he's saving for later in the week.
entries.text: With one lantern lit, half the bench sits in shadow. Went into the scrap pile for a flat piece of tin to stand behind the lantern and throw the light back; pulled a hand-wide piece out and the sheet above it slid down onto the rest with a clatter.
entries.title: Digging for tin

entries.onMind: hammering it flat in the morning
entries.text: The piece is the right size but one corner is folded over and the face is dented like a spoon. It'll throw light everywhere but where I want it until I hammer it flat on the vise in daylight.
entries.title: Bent corner

entries.onMind: how many days the bundle has left
entries.text: Ate a slice of the bread and a sliver of cheese on the crate. The loaf is under half now, so the acorn halves in the creek will have to carry more of the load.
entries.title: Bread and cheese

entries.onMind: the blank half of the sheet
entries.text: Laid the sheet on the bench beside the dome and drew an arrow parallel to the sliver, crescent and dot at its head the way we mark it at home, infinity mark for east. Where west goes on the arrow there is no mark, like every compass back home.
entries.title: North on paper

entries.text: Back home they would say the blank side of the sheet is right, nothing there to draw. All I have paced west of the creek is sixty-one steps to a stump, and it was trees the whole way. Sixty-one paces isn't much of an answer.
entries.title: Sixty-one paces

entries.text: Twisted an arm-length of cord on the crate, rolling it on my thigh and doubling it back. That was the last of the dry fiber in the bundle; the stalks on the bank want another stripping.
entries.title: Last of the fiber

entries.text: Got six turns round the rear side-spar joint before the cord ran out, one short of the front joint and no frapping turn. Tied it off. It'll do for a test or it won't.
entries.title: Rear joint, short

entries.onMind: whether the other fire is going out
entries.text: Ate a handful of halves out of the net bag by lantern; nine and a half hours in the current and I had to go looking for the bitter. Past the water the orange glow is down to a dull red, no flame and no sparks tonight.
entries.title: Hunting for the bitter

entries.reason: The rear joint got six turns and no frapping turn before the cord ran out.
entries.text: Filed a notch a cord's width around the end of a scrap spar at the bench. If turns sitting down in a notch hold where seven on smooth wood slide, the rear joint can live with six until I strip more stalks.
entries.title: A test notch

entries.text: Sat on the crate with the lantern turned down low. In daylight I'll take the sheet and the pencil past the stump and keep pacing until something stops me, then draw whatever it is.
entries.title: Past the stump

entries.text: Out of cord, so I took the twine off the paper roll and wound five turns of it down into the notch on the scrap spar. Past the water, the dull red I saw from the shallows is gone; whoever keeps that fire put it to bed.
entries.title: Twine off the roll

entries.text: Clamped the scrap spar in the vise and hung off it. The turns in the notch didn't move a hair. On the second hang the wood split from the bottom of the notch along the grain, a crack as long as my finger.
entries.title: Holds cord, not wood

entries.text: So a notch holds the cord and costs the wood. If one goes in the real rear spar it can be no deeper than the twine is thick, or I'm trading one weak joint for another.
entries.title: No deeper than twine

entries.text: Looked at the lid under the dome side-on by lantern. Hours under the glass and the water still humps over the rim; without it, it sank in an evening. No wind tonight to tell me anything about the gap.
entries.title: Still humped

entries.text: Ate two handfuls of halves out of the net bag by lantern, and the bitter is nearly gone. Bed early. Tomorrow the blank side of the sheet.
entries.title: Barely bitter

entries.onMind: the blank side of the sheet
entries.text: Set the flat stone back on the net bag. The clouds have broken up over the creek and there are stars in the gap above the water, the first clear patch since I made camp.
entries.title: Stars over the water
